articles.summary: As a performer, Tim Curry knew how to walk a fine line. Even his most sinister characters had an ironic sort of appeal, because watching Curry have fun is, in itself, fun. The actor, who died yesterday at age 80, acted with palpable glee: He could produce a real-life version of the Grinch’s ever-widening grin and could commit to sheer silliness in a way that freed him to twirl around in a cape while singing a gibberish song about Halloween . Perhaps nowhere was this more evident than in the 1985 film Clue . When the raucous comedy adaptation of the classic whodunit board game debuted in theaters, Paramount Pictures had a unique plan: Instead of one ending, the movie would have three, and audiences never knew which resolution—which killer, in which room, with which weapon—they were going to see. How could the studio sell viewers on a story as convoluted as Clue , whose script was designed to keep people guessing until the very last second? By recruiting an ensemble of comedy greats led by Curry, of course. The actor could easily inhabit a character who was neither wholly a hero nor totally a villain, but rather a merrily odd mix of both. [ Read: The absolute pleasure of Tim Curry ]

articles.summary: Because this week evidently decided it hadn’t already taken enough beloved 80-year-olds from us , Tim Curry passed away Tuesday night. A king of camp, many remember Curry for scene-stealing roles in movies like Clue , The Rocky Horror Picture Show , and of course, Muppet Treasure Island . But he also loved popping up in video games, a perfect fit for his inimitably over-the-top stylings. According to Moby Games , Curry ultimately appeared in 22 games. Supporters believe joining the European bloc could give the country greater protection and boost its economy, while critics worry over sovereignty. The Arctic has emerged as a key battleground between global superpowers: Trump has threatened to take over Greenland, an autonomous territory belonging to Denmark. Jeremiah Harding was not done with the Spokane County Commission by the end of its August 25 meeting. Other folks trickled out of the room, but Harding, dressed in a red flannel and a T-shirt splattered with paint from his day job as a laborer and a smart phone on a selfie stick in hand, approached the commissioners as they shuffled their papers and prepared to leave. Commissioner Al French quickly gathered his things and walked out. Everyone else stayed to see what Harding wanted. “Are any of you gonna answer Brittany’s question?” he said. Harding was referencing Brittany Anderson, the Spokanite who released a trove of documents in July that showed French had been in high-level secret discussions with a data center developer to build a facility on the West Plains — for months. articles.author: Rogé Karma
articles.summary: Sign up for Work in Progress , a newsletter where Rogé Karma investigates the mysteries of a complicated economy. America’s biggest AI companies have spent the past few years churning out advanced new models as fast as they possibly can. Now the industry is screaming out with a nearly unified voice: Please, for the love of God, make us slow down.
